rationale: B wins because it keeps the floors separate: announcement, channel thesis, retailer-format story, product story. A has good bones, but it keeps putting stage makeup on thin facts with lines like "after a decade of treating retail as the enemy" and "the one who never made it to the prestige mall." B's line "It only stands apart if the Kohl's door count is real and material" is the editorial discipline here: it knows which angles are real and which need proof before anyone embarrasses themselves.
gaps_in_A: "after a decade of treating retail as the enemy" overclaims the facts. DTC-only is in the update; anti-retail ideology is not.
"the one who never made it to the prestige mall" invents a shopper profile. Sephora at Kohl's is named, but no demographic or geographic data is supplied.

It wrongly refuses "Glossier launches three-product fragrance line alongside Sephora expansion." First fragrance line extension plus 800 more Sephora doors is a valid narrow fragrance-trade angle if product details and distribution are confirmed.

The first two kept angles lean on the same core fact: "wholesale is now its fastest-growing channel." Trend versus contrarian is defensible, but the set needs clearer separation or one will eat the other in pitching.
gaps_in_B: "in one step" is a little too neat. The update says the expansion is being announced; it does not provide rollout cadence.
"The prevailing belief in that world" imports outside context. It is useful framing, but it needs sourcing before it becomes a pitch claim.
"The number is the story" is true for trade, but thin. Without Sephora confirmation, rollout timing, and door split, that angle dies after a routine brief.
The fragrance angle is smart but still conditional: without product names, prices, formats, exclusivity, and door availability, it is not pitch-ready.
